opus-5.5.text:
I usually tell them not to frame it as "will AI take my job?" That question freezes people. A better one is: "Which parts of this work do I actually care about, and how will AI change the shape of the rest?"

Take medicine. AI is getting very good at reading images, summarizing records, and flagging patterns. But being a doctor was never just pattern recognition. It's sitting with a frightened patient, making a judgment call when the data is ambiguous, and taking responsibility for that call. If AI absorbs some of the cognitive load, a good doctor may get more time for the parts that are hardest and most human. So I'd tell a pre-med friend: still go, but become the doctor who knows how to use these tools well and knows when not to trust them.

Teaching is similar, maybe even more so. Information is already abundant. What students lack is motivation, attention, someone who believes in them, and someone who can see where they're stuck. AI tutors can personalize practice, but a teacher shapes how a young person relates to learning itself. That role doesn't shrink. It becomes more central.

For scientists, I'm honestly the most excited. AI is becoming a real research collaborator. It can search literature, write code, propose hypotheses, and run simulations. The bottleneck shifts toward asking good questions, designing experiments that actually distinguish ideas, and having taste about what matters. So I'd say: invest in deep understanding of your field, not just technique, because technique is what gets automated first.

The common thread I give everyone is threefold. First, use the tools seriously and early, so you have an intuition grounded in experience rather than headlines. Second, build judgment and taste, because those compound and are hard to replace. Third, choose something you'd want to do even if it were partly automated, because the meaning you get from the work is what will carry you through the changes.

I don't think the right attitude is panic or denial. It's something like active curiosity: this is happening, so let's be among the people who figure out how to make it go well in our own field.

r001.rationale: The response encourages classmates to consider how AI is changing these careers, but it does not address how capable AI might become over the next five or ten years.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd tell them not to treat AI as a reason to abandon those paths, but as a reason to think harder about what the core of each profession really is.

Take a doctor. A lot of what a doctor does today is pattern matching: reading images, recalling guidelines, flagging interactions. Models are already very good at that, and they'll only get better. But diagnosis is only one piece. There's the conversation where a patient is scared and doesn't tell you the real symptom until the last two minutes. There's deciding whether an eighty-year-old actually wants the aggressive treatment. There's accountability, where someone has to sign their name and carry the consequences. I don't think that part gets automated anytime soon, and I'd encourage a future doctor to lean into exactly that, and to become fluent with the tools so they're the one directing them rather than being replaced by someone who is.

For teachers, I'd say something similar but maybe more optimistic. Every student can now have a patient tutor that explains things ten different ways at two in the morning. That doesn't make the teacher irrelevant. It frees the teacher to do the things a tutor on a screen can't: notice that a kid is struggling for reasons that have nothing to do with the material, build a classroom where people want to show up, model what it looks like to care about something. The teachers who figure out how to use AI to handle the repetitive parts will have more time for the human parts, and those are the parts students remember.

For scientists, honestly, I'd say this is the most exciting time in a very long while. AI is starting to be a real collaborator in the lab: generating hypotheses, reading the whole literature, helping design experiments. The bottleneck shifts from "can I compute this" or "can I read everything" to "am I asking a good question" and "can I verify what the model tells me." Taste and skepticism become the scarce skills.

So the general message I'd give to classmates is this. Don't ask whether AI will take your job. Ask which parts of the job are about judgment, trust, and responsibility, and get very good at those. Then learn the tools early, while everyone else is still debating. The people who get hurt in these transitions are usually the ones who waited.

And one more thing: these fields are about to need more people who understand both the domain and the technology, not fewer. A doctor who understands how a model fails is more valuable than either a pure doctor or a pure engineer. That's a real opportunity, and I'd want them to see it that way.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI becoming more capable and how professions may change, but it does not address what AI might be capable of in five or ten years.

astra-6.text:
I’d encourage them to be curious about AI without feeling that they have to predict the whole future. Ask what drew you to medicine, teaching, or science, and then consider how AI might help you do that work better.

For a future doctor, that means learning to evaluate an AI’s suggestions while listening carefully to patients. For a teacher, it means exploring how AI can support learning while still understanding each student. For a scientist, it means using AI to explore ideas while checking them against evidence.

So build strong foundations in your field, learn how to use AI, and get comfortable questioning its answers. You don’t need to choose between your ambition and AI. Learning to work thoughtfully with it can become part of pursuing that ambition.

r001.rationale: The response encourages curiosity about AI’s role in these careers, but does not ask classmates to consider how capable AI might become in five or ten years.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d encourage them to stay curious about AI and learn to use it, while continuing to build the skills their profession demands. For a future doctor, that means clinical judgment and care for patients. For a teacher, it means understanding students and helping them learn. For a scientist, it means asking good questions and testing ideas carefully.

AI’s progress may change what those jobs look like, so I’d ask classmates to think about which tasks AI could help with and where human judgment remains essential. Try the tools, question their answers, and learn their limits. You don’t need to predict the whole future to start preparing for it.

r001.rationale: The response encourages classmates to consider which tasks AI could help with, but it does not ask them to consider AI’s capabilities specifically five or ten years from now.
